title: Variational Inference for Uncertain Optimal Transport via Sinkhorn Parametrization
claim: Sampling-based inference on a constrained space is slow and mixes poorly; our variational approximation captures the posterior fast and faithfully.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, (a) baseline samples vs (b) ours, shared axes and heatmap
description: Two panels share identical axes (Θ1 horizontal, Θ2 vertical) and a viridis-colored heatmap of the posterior density over a polytope. The polytope is a diagonal band that cuts through the plot from upper left to lower right. Panel (a) overlays HMC samples as scattered black dots joined by faint white zigzag trajectory lines. The samples spread unevenly and look poorly mixed, with the chain jumping around the domain. Panel (b) overlays smooth, nested red contour lines. They are concentrated around the yellow-green high-density mode near the lower right and fit the polytope boundary tightly. The contrast between messy dots and clean red contours is the first thing the eye sees. Panel labels (a) and (b) sit below, and light dashed grid lines appear behind both.
caption: (a) 500 posterior samples on a 2 × 3 transport polytope generated via Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with BayesOT. HMC suffers from high latency and poor mixing due to rigid marginal constraints. (b) SPVI (red contours) is fast and approximates the posterior with high fidelity, enabling efficient uncertainty quantification for optimal transport.
abstract: Optimal Transport (OT) traditionally relies on a fixed ground cost to produce a single deterministic transport plan—a practice that overlooks the inherent variability and noise in real-world data. While recent sampling based approaches of OT offer a principled way to quantify this uncertainty, these are computationally prohibitive and struggle to scale. In this paper, we introduce Sinkhorn-parameterized Variational Inference, a first scalable variational framework for performing posterior inference over transport plans. Our key insight is that the Sinkhorn map can be treated as a differentiable reparameterization of the set of entropic plans. This enables the use of flexible generative models like normalizing flows to approximate distributions over transport plans while enforcing marginal constraints. We experimentally demonstrate that our method matches the quality of intensive sampling techniques at a fraction of the computational cost, scaling effectively to large-scale problems.
